newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria's lev has almost 120-year history.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's lev has almost 120-year history.

text.p: Bulgaria's 120-year old currency added another chapter to its history on Tuesday when the lev was pegged to the mark in a currency board system as part of an arrangement with the International Monetary Fund.
Bulgaria has come a long way since independence in 1878. For two years after independence, Bulgaria denominated state budgets in French francs because it did not yet have a currency.

The Bulgarian National Bank was established on January 25, 1879, less than a year after the end of Ottoman rule, but parliament did not approve the Mintage Law until May 27, 1880 to establish the lev as the national currency.
But even after 1880, Russian roubles, Turkish lira, Romanian lei, Serbian dinars, French francs and other European currencies remained legal tender for several years.
Lev name means lion, which is the animal depicted on Bulgaria's coat of arms. It was divided into 100 stotinki, borrowed from the French centime.

Early lev coins were gold or silver, but gold coins quickly disappeared from circulation as Bulgarians squirrelled them away as a valuable asset, and trade was serviced by silver and less valuable coins made of copper, nickel and alloys.
Ferdinand Saxe Coburg-Gotha was the first Bulgarian king to appear on silver coins minted in 1891 and gold coins in 1894.
In 1885, as the economy developed, the Bulgarian National Bank was authorised to issue banknotes to ease payments.
A third of their value had to be covered by gold kept in central bank vaults, and the bank was obliged to pay on demand the equivalent amount of gold to any note bearer.

But the central bank stopped exchanging notes for gold in 1899 for two years when economic crisis emerged at the end of the 19th century and forced it to start substituting the gold standard for a silver standard to preserve depleted reserves.
In 1912, exchanging notes for gold and silver permanently ended when Bulgaria went into the First Balkan War.

The need for small denomination notes rose during World War One as silver, copper and nickel coins disappeared from circulation. As a result, the central bank issued one and two lev notes printed in Germany.
Bulgaria's first 1,000 lev note was printed in New York and went into circulation in 1923. The first 5,000 lev notes appeared in 1924 but were withdrawn two years later after forgeries were detected.
Notes issued in 1943 depicted for the first and last time King Simeon II, then aged six. He went into exile in 1946 after the Soviet Red Army installed a communist regime and now lives in Madrid.
His son Prince Kiril, who works for investment bank Lehman Brothers International, is an economic adviser to popular reformist president Petar Stoyanov, who took office in January.

A run on the lev and the collapse of the banking system in 1996 triggered another economic crisis, bringing down the Socialist government and forcing the lev to plunge below 3,000 to the dollar in February.
Notes of ever larger denominations have been put into circulation to ease cash payments as inflation soared, and stotinki coins have been scrapped.
The last communist-era banknotes still bearing the hammer and sickle were withdrawn last year. The highest value note now is 50,000 levs, which went into circulation last month.
